title: Research Bite #82: Debunking the Learning Styles Neuromyth
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's Research Bite #82 breaks down a Greek study by Papadatou-Pastou, Touloumakos and Theotokatou that tested the learning styles hypothesis with 194 primary pupils aged 10 to 12. Pupils identified their style in two ways, then learned three weather topics in three formats (pictures with text, narration only, or pictures and text with narration) and took a ten-question quiz after each. Matching the format to the pupil's supposed style made no reliable difference, scoring 65.5 percent when matched and 63.0 percent when not, and the crossover pattern the hypothesis predicts never appeared. The combined audiovisual format won for every group, at about 72 percent. Barton translates this into classroom advice: drop the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic labels, talk through any diagram you show, and treat pupils' own claims about their style with caution because the two identification methods often disagreed. He also lists limitations, including the immediate multiple-choice test, too few kinaesthetic pupils to analyse, and a single Greek region.
points: Matching instruction to a pupil's preferred modality produced no benefit, so separate task versions for visual or auditory types are effort without payoff.
The strongest result was for combining modalities, since pictures with spoken explanation beat either format alone for every style group.
Pupils' self-labels were unreliable, with only 64 of 106 self-described visual learners classed as visual by the questionnaire.
Barton flags a wellbeing risk that labels may teach pupils they are poor at learning from certain formats, and recommends choosing format by content instead.
He suggests auditing CPD, SEND guidance and observation forms for lingering learning-styles language, citing evidence that about a quarter of teacher-training textbooks recommend matching.
quotes: Teaching pupils in their supposed learning style made no difference to how much they remembered. Showing pictures while explaining aloud raised scores for every style group.

Pupils did no better when the format matched their style, and the crossover pattern the hypothesis predicts never appeared. Pictures and text with narration beat both single-sense formats for every group.
Stop sorting pupils into visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners. Pupils scored 65.5% on the quiz when the format matched their style and 63.0% when it didn’t, a gap too small to be reliable.

Show the picture and talk through it at the same time. The combined format, which added recorded narration to the pictures and text, produced the highest scores (around 72%, compared with 66% for pictures and text alone and 62% for narration alone).

Only 64 of the 106 pupils who called themselves visual learners were classed as visual by the questionnaire. The authors suggest a preferred format may simply feel easier without helping pupils remember more.
Learning was measured by a multiple-choice quiz immediately after eight-minute lessons, so it did not test longer-term memory or deeper understanding.

When you choose a format, base the choice on the content (a diagram for the water cycle, a recording for pronunciation in a language lesson) and say so to the class, so pupils hear that the material drives the choice.
